transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-14
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Julia Park (Redwood AE), Marcus Lee (Redwood SE), Ana Gomez (Redwood CSM), Ethan Cole (CTO, RocketTech), Priya Nair (Lead Engineer), Samir Venkatesh (DevOps), Liu Chen (Security)

Summary: quick hands-on SDK install, auth flow, console walk, and initial Optimize recommendations. Customer wants private-like controls, worried about encryption/KMS and VPC peering. We agreed to provide sandbox creds and security pack.

Topics: SDK install (py/ts), API key and env var patterns, SSO/SAML, VPC peering considerations, Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs, Optimize suggestions (batching, quantize), next steps and benchmarks

Action items (auto): see metadata above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Julia (AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, looks like most of us are here, i'll do a 2 minute intro then hand to Marcus for the SDK walk though and then we can pair on auth.
[00:12] Ethan (CTO): thanks julia, appreciate the time — we've got Priya and Samir on to run the actual install, Liu from security is here for the compliance bits.
[00:20] Marcus (SE): cool, i'll share my screen in a sec. first quick question, what's the target env? staging in AWS, on prem, or hybrid?
[00:30] Priya (Lead Eng): staging in AWS, eventually hybrid but initial pilot in us-west-2. we prefer python for the inference pipeline but the front end prototype uses typescript.
[00:40] Marcus (SE): great, that'll map cleanly to our py and ts SDKs. quick note: i'll go through the python quickstart first, show auth, then TS example for the frontend.
[01:05] Samir (DevOps): one ask from me — we need to understand VPC peering, or private endpoint setup. also curious about KMS integration for keys and token rotation.
[01:20] Julia (AE): perfect, security is important — we'll cover KMS/HSM, SSO, and audit logs in the security pack. liu, feel free to interject.
[01:28] Liu (Security): sounds good, i'd like to see where logs are stored and retention controls as well as SAML federation.
[01:35] Marcus (SE): okay share screen, opening the quickstart repo. so our python SDK install is pip install redwood-inference-sdk, then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in env, or use a credentials file. i'll paste the snippet in chat.
[02:05] (typing noises, short pause)
[02:12] Marcus (SE): quick starter code: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); res = client.generate("Summarize ticket: ...", max_tokens=256) — result prints. note: in some environments the env var pattern is REDWOOD_KEY or REDWOOD_API_KEY depending on the buildpack; we try to normalize but you may see both.
[02:45] Priya: slight question — we have CI that injects secrets via vault, do you support mounting secrets or do you recommend pipeline envs?
[02:55] Marcus (SE): both work. for CI we see teams use vault + env injection. if you use our dedicated/private offering you can also integrate with KMS to rotate keys and use short-lived tokens for pods.
[03:20] Julia (AE): just to clarify, short lived tokens for Dedicated and Private deployments are part of our enterprise integrations. Hosted also supports token rotation but you manage the key material.
[03:40] Ethan: can you explain the difference again between Hosted and Dedicated for performance and cost?
[03:48] Marcus (SE): sure. Hosted is fastest to get started, consumption billing, good for prototypes. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools, predictable throughput, and isolation — better for consistent latency, and allows private network peering. cost wise Dedicated is commit-based so unit cost goes down at scale but requires contract.
[04:15] Priya: and Private?
[04:18] Marcus (SE): Private is customer-managed control plane, VPC or on-prem options, full network isolation, integrates with customer KMS/HSM. slightly more ops on your side but required for regulated workloads.
[04:40] Liu (Security): any gap in SSO/SAML? we use Okta with SCIM for provisioning.
[04:48] Julia: we support SAML SSO and SCIM, RBAC roles, and audit logs. our security pack will include snapshots of our SOC2, ISO docs and network diagrams.
[05:08] Marcus (SE): ok back to SDK. switching to a TS example. for frontend you can use the browser SDK with token exchange or a server-side TS call. example: import { Redwood } from '@redwood/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); client.chat.create(...). note in browser flows you should use short-lived proxy tokens.
[06:05] Priya: we run a mix of SSR and client side. is there a recommended pattern?
[06:12] Marcus: SSR for the heavy-lifting is safer — keep keys server-side and do browser streaming via a token exchange endpoint.
[06:30] (brief crosstalk)
[07:00] Marcus: next, Console quick tour. i'll open the Console. on the left is Models, Routes, and Optimize. Routes map an API route to a model version, you can configure batching window and overrides.
[07:20] Marcus: Optimize recommendations live under the Optimize tab — based on observed latency and token sizes we may suggest quantized variants or change batch window to hit your latency SLO. for example, if your median seq length is 64 tokens, we might recommend 8-bit quantization with continuous batching of up to 8 concurrent requests.
[07:55] Priya: what about KV cache? we use long context with embeddings and want to avoid re-encoding.
[08:02] Marcus: we support prefix caching and kv cache for decoder-only models; might appear in the console as "KV cache" or sometimes transcribed in older exports as key V cache — just a naming quirk. caching reduces tokens charged and latency for repeated prefixes.
[08:25] Ethan: latency numbers — what should we assume for a 256 token generation on a dedicated 80GB A100 equivalent?
[08:35] Marcus: rough baseline is 200-300ms per 64 tokens after warmup when using optimized kernels; 256 tokens could be ~900ms-1.2s depending on batch and quantization. we'll run a specific baseline for you.
[09:05] Marcus: i'll also demo streaming in the SDK — generating chunked responses so the frontend can render progressive output.
[09:30] (demo playback)
[10:12] Priya: tiny nit — the pip package name is redwood-inference-sdk? we saw redwood-sdk in a doc earlier.
[10:20] Marcus: yes sorry for the confusion, top-level name is redwood-inference-sdk for python; TS package is @redwood/sdk. docs have both but some older samples used shorthand redwood-sdk. we'll standardize the quickstart.
[11:00] Liu: on audit logs, retention is configurable? we need 7 years for some customers.
[11:10] Julia: retention defaults are shorter but enterprise add-on supports extended retention — we'll include options in the security pack and a pricing note.
[11:30] Ethan: about data residency — we require EU and US regions for different products. is region pinning supported?
[11:38] Marcus: yes, you can pin model hosting to regions, and Dedicated/Private can be provisioned in target regions. hosted model catalog shows availability per region.
[12:05] Samir: for the VPC peering, do you support AWS PrivateLink or classic peering?
[12:12] Marcus: both patterns are supported; PrivateLink for secure endpoint access is typical. for Dedicated we usually do VPC peering and cross-account roles, for Private we can provide an AMI or on-prem package.
[12:40] Priya: let's try a quick hands-on install — i'll follow along and pip install.
[12:45] (typing)
[13:05] Priya: install completed, now setting REDWOOD_API_KEY via our CI vault local setup.
[13:20] Marcus: perfect. run the sample generate with max_tokens=128. when you run keep an eye on the token count and the returned latency.
[13:40] Priya: running now...
[13:55] (short pause)
[14:05] Priya: got a response, latency about 420ms, result looks good.
[14:12] Marcus: nice, that's without batching and on our hosted sandbox — good baseline.
[14:30] Ethan: Marcus, about metrics — can we export traces to our datadog?
[14:38] Marcus: yes we expose traces and you can pipe to datadog/jaeger with our trace hooks or use our Console for token-level breakdowns.
[15:00] (timestamp jump)
[20:00] Marcus: switching to Optimize advice — if your common prompt pattern is a 32 token instruction plus a 224 token response we typically recommend target batch size 6-12 and quantization for cost savings. optimize console shows recommended profiles with expected latency and cost delta.
[20:45] Priya: curious about regressions — if you quantize model and accuracy dips, what's the rollback path?
[20:53] Marcus: Console has rollouts — canary and A/B with automatic fallback. if quality drops beyond a threshold we auto rollback to previous model variant. you can configure thresholds per route.
[21:30] Liu: from compliance POV, can rollouts be audited?
[21:35] Julia: yes rollouts and config changes are logged; we'll show you an example audit export in the pack.
[22:00] Samir: one more infra question — what's the most minimal CIDR we need to open for peering?
[22:08] Marcus: usually one /28 for control plane stuff and a few additional ranges for worker subnets; we'll send a sample diagram with exact ports and ranges.
[23:00] (short break noises)
[25:30] Priya: Marcus, i wanted to ask about embeddings — we use embeddings for reranking, are there batching knobs?
[25:40] Marcus: embeddings support bulk endpoints; batching is more efficient and we have a dedicated embedding route that will process several thousand vectors in a single call. cost/perf profiles are in Optimize.
[26:05] Ethan: any known gaps with our stack? we use k8s, vault, okta, datadog.
[26:12] Marcus: that's a common stack and supported. vault for secrets, okta for SAML/SCIM, k8s integration with sidecar token injection for pods is well documented.
[26:45] Priya: can we run a week-long POC with limited Dedicated capacity?
[26:55] Julia: yes we can do a short trial and a small Dedicated pool for benchmarking — we'll surface pricing. usually that requires a short commit but we can do a limited pilot contract.
[27:20] Ethan: timing — we want to decide this quarter, so quick follow-ups would help.
[27:30] Julia: understood, we'll prioritize the sandbox creds and the security pack this week.
[28:00] Marcus: quick note about model selection — Console shows Redwood-verified models and open families; for inference speed we have optimized kernels for decoder-only and encoder-decoder variants. sometimes model names are abbreviate or mis-typed in older exports like 'redwod-model' — ignore those.
[28:42] Priya: ok switching to TS quick test. Samir, you'll watch network bits.
[29:00] (typing, demo)
[30:15] Priya: TS example succeeded, streaming worked fine in our SSR test.
[30:30] Marcus: great. i'll attach the TS sample to the ticket.
[31:05] Liu: follow-up security question — do you store customer prompts for quality monitoring?
[31:12] Julia: by default hosted logs may store prompts for a short period to run quality monitoring, but you can opt-out or enable prompt redaction. Dedicated/Private gives you control over retention.
[31:40] Liu: any PII redaction tools?
[31:45] Marcus: we have a PII redaction layer you can enable; it can be applied at ingress to strip sensitive fields. we'll include configuration examples.
[32:10] Priya: for the bench test Marcus will run, what input should we send? typical is a 5-10k daily users sim; but for the first pass maybe run 100 req/sec of 256 token avg.
[32:25] Marcus: that sounds good. send us a representative prompt set and we'll run both hosted sandbox and a small Dedicated pool to show delta.
[33:00] Ethan: do you do contractually backed SLOs for latency?
[33:07] Julia: Dedicated has SLA options for uptime and latency tiers in enterprise agreements. Hosted has best-effort plus published performance profiles.
[33:25] Priya: are there any gotchas for serverless environments? cold starts?
[33:32] Marcus: cold start for serverless to our hosted endpoints is minimal — but for large models the first few requests may be slower as kernels warm. that's where batching and prefix caching help.
[34:00] (several quick clarifications)
[36:00] Marcus: i'm going to summarize recommended config for your pilot: 1) python SDK with env-secret injection via vault, 2) SSR pattern for front end with token exchange, 3) small Dedicated pool (2 x GPU) for baseline and then scale, 4) enable KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts, 5) Optimize profile: quantize to int8 for cost savings and batch size 8 with 50ms window.
[36:40] Priya: that sounds actionable. Marcus, can you produce an initial config file we can drop into k8s?
[36:48] Marcus: yes i'll produce a k8s manifest with example secrets mount and a sample route config.
[37:10] Julia: next steps recap — we'll: send sandbox creds and quickstart repo, attach SOC2/security pack + network diagram, Marcus to run baseline tests and share results, schedule follow up for Dedicated pilot.
[37:30] Ethan: timeline — we aim to choose by end of July so please prioritize.
[37:40] Julia: noted. we'll target the sandbox creds by 2025-07-16 and baseline results by 2025-07-21.
[38:00] (wrap up chatter)
[40:00] Priya: one last question — is there an in-console cost estimator?
[40:08] Marcus: yes Optimize includes a cost estimator per route that projects monthly spend given request volumes and token sizes.
[40:30] Liu: ok thanks team, we'll review the security pack and get back with any follow ups.
[41:00] Julia: thanks everyone — we'll follow up in the ticket with links.
[41:20] (meeting ends, casual signoffs)

Recap (automated): sandbox keys, quickstart repo, security docs + SOC2, bench plan, k8s manifest, scheduled follow-up for dedicated pilot.

Notes on transcription: some brand names and internal product names occasionally mistranscribed (e.g., "key V cache" instead of KV cache). occasional speaker overlap and short filler words present.
